en: K1, K4: Checked 10: Rājasūya [no repetition at the end of the paṭala]
In the cool season, he burns the dry grass;
in spring they become productive. Fifteen days from here, on the full moon of Phālguna, he undergoes initiation.

There is one initiation (*dīkṣā*), three *upasads*, and the Soma-pressing (*prasuta*) takes place on the fifth day; thus this Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma is concluded. It has gold as its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), serves as a means of purification (*pavitra*), and constitutes the ten-day period from here. On the full moon day, he offers a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) to Anumati.
Those [stakes] which fall short of the yoke-pin (śamyā) on the near side, with those he prepares a cake on one potsherd for Nirṛti; if they do not fall short, he should remove them,
or he prepares them at the joints of the black [stalks] or at the joints of the withered ones.
Pointing toward these directions—the south and the west—they seek out their own-made pit, a chasm, or a water-vessel. By way of the southwest (Nairṛta), they go further away.
Having placed a single-mouthed vessel upon their own-made saline wasteland, he adds fuel.

Or, at a chasm, or at a black spot, or at two joints, or at a fissure, having placed [the vessel] between his two thumbs with the words, "This is thy portion, O Nirṛti," he offers the oblation with: "Thou art possessed of the oblation, O Being; release this one from distress, Svāhā!"
A black garment is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Having sprinkled [the water], they return without looking back, saying, "Svāhā! Homage to him who did this!
Having returned, he offers a spoonful of oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire. He proceeds with the *ānumata* rite and gives a cow as a gift. This sacrifice is completed.
They dwell [there].
In the morning, he offers a *caru* oblation to Āditya and gives a choice gift.
This sacrifice concludes;
they dwell [there].
In the morning, he causes [them] to drink... (11)... he offers.
The *vāmana* sacrifice for Vahīndra... [the sacrifice] for Vahīndra... this is the sacrifice; they dwell [there]. In the morning, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Soma.
He gives gold;
this sacrifice is completed, and they dwell [there]. In the morning, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra.
He gives a bull as a sacrificial gift. This sacrifice concludes; they remain [there]. In the morning, he offers an oblation on eight potsherds to Agni.
[He offers] a *vaiśvadeva* oblation of boiled rice (*caru*) with twelve [portions]. He gives a first-born calf. At dawn, he pours out [grain for] a *saumya* oblation of *śyāmāka* millet;
he gives a garment.
On the day of the Santis, he offers a pap of cooked rice to Sarasvatī;
he gives a young cow as a gift; on the day of the Santis.
In the morning, he offers a *caru* oblation to Sarasvat;
he gives a young bull as a gift.
The [rite] concludes... if they should encounter others...
They sacrifice with the *ārambhaṇīyā* oblation for Sarasvatī and Sarasvant.
If they do not reach their goal, they perform the two Sarasvat oblations day after day; on the following day, they sacrifice with the *ārambhaṇīyā* oblation.
On the day they sacrifice with the *ārambhaṇīyā* oblation, they dwell there for the night and do not sacrifice again that day.
They dwell.
In the morning, he sacrifices with the Full Moon sacrifice.
They dwell.
In the morning, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman;
its fuel consists of well-purified wood-shavings.
They stay overnight.

In the morning, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Aṃhomuc. He sacrifices with its two *aprī* verses and two oblations in alternating succession; he sacrifices with the *aprī* verses and the oblations in their proper order.
On the new moon day itself, he performs the new moon sacrifice.
On the full moon day, he approaches the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice;
he performs the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices,
and having sacrificed with them, he gives away a chariot yoked with white horses and bearing white reins.
This is the sacrificial fee for Sutrāman;
this is his source. Through the two leadings... he attains them by means of the oblations; with those Sākamedha rites, he sacrifices. Through the two leadings...
he attains them by means of the oblations; with those Sākamedha rites, he sacrifices.
Having sacrificed with those black [animals], he gives a chariot that is yoked but not driven. This is the *dakṣiṇā* for the *Aṃhomuc* sacrifice;
this is its source. He thus overcomes the blindness of his eyes through these two oblations; indeed, he performs the entire Kārtika sacrifice by means of these two offerings.
He attains the Śunāsīrīya; with that he sacrifices.
Having sacrificed with it, he gives a team of twelve oxen to the Adhvaryu and departs.

With these very two oblations, he performs the sacrifice throughout the entire month of Mārgaśīrṣa and for twenty-five nights of Taiṣa; he offers the *rathendraturīya* oblation, consisting of a cake on eight potsherds for Agni. <10.2> (10.2.1) [K4,69b5–;M327–8]

He offers a *raudra* oblation of *gavīdhuka* grain, a *aindra* oblation of curd, and a *vāruṇa* oblation of barley; he gives a *vahinī* cow as a sacrificial gift. This sacrifice is concluded. They dwell there.

In the morning, whichever of those two oblations has its time, when the *prāśitra* portion has been set aside, he spreads out the embers of the Āhavanīya fire and places five fuel-sticks upon them: a *palāśa* stick in the east, a *nyagrodha* stick in the south, an *aśvattha* stick in the west, an *audumbara* stick in the north, and a *plakṣa* stick in the middle; these he offers with the five verses beginning, "Those gods who sit in the front."

He makes an offering with the fivefold-grasped ladle, saying, "The Rakṣas is subdued! He places them in the middle, saying, "The Rakṣas is burnt up! Here I consume the Rakṣases! He offers five spoonfuls with the formulas: "To Agni, the slayer of Rakṣases, svāhā! To Yama, the slayer of Rakṣases, svāhā! To Savitṛ, the slayer of Rakṣases, svāhā! To Varuṇa, the slayer of Rakṣases, svāhā! To Bṛhaspati, the slayer of Rakṣases, svāhā!"

"To the one who possesses swift horses, the slayer of Rākṣasas, Svāhā!"—with these words he gives away a chariot drawn by a pair of mares. This sacrifice is concluded; following its conclusion, [he offers] groats of *apāmārga* grass.

He prepares a *sruva*-ladle made of *palāśa* wood toward this northern-western direction. They seek out a natural depression or a fissure. With *apāmārga* flour, they go forth toward a water-vessel. Having placed a single fire-stick (*ekormuka*) in a self-made salt-flat or in a fissure, he adds fuel with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," using a *palāśa* stick.

With the *sruva* ladle, he offers groats of *apāmārga* grass, saying: "By the arms of the Aśvins, I offer the slaying of the Rākṣasa, svāhā!"—"The Rākṣasa is slain! May you slay him! [M: "May you slay the Rākṣasa"].

Saying "Protect!", he sprinkles the *sruva* ladle; whatever he wears, that he gives away. Having sprinkled water around, they return without looking back. This much is the ritual action for this day. They dwell there. In the morning, he offers the *devikā* oblations: a cake on twelve potsherds for Dhātṛ, a pap for Anumati, a pap for Rākā, a pap for Sinīvālī, and a pap for Kuhū. He gives a pair of cattle. This sacrifice is concluded. They dwell there.

In the morning, he offers the first oblation of the Triṣaṃyukta rites: a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Viṣṇu, and a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu; he gives a dwarf draft-ox as a gift. This sacrifice is completed. They remain overnight. In the morning, he offers the second oblation of the Triṣaṃyukta rites: a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Soma, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Soma, and a pap for Soma; he gives a brown ox as a gift. This sacrifice is completed. They remain overnight.
In the morning, he offers the third oblation consisting of threefold combinations: a pap of cooked rice for Soma and Pūṣan, and one for Indra and Pūṣan.

He offers a *caru* oblation to Pūṣan and gives a dark-colored bull as a gift. This sacrifice is completed; they stay overnight. In the morning, he offers a twelve-potherd cake (*dvādaśakapāla*) to Vaiśvānara and gives gold as a gift. This sacrifice is completed; they stay overnight. In the morning, he offers a barley *caru* to Varuṇa and gives a horse as a gift. This sacrifice is completed. On this day, they conclude with the sacrifice to Varuṇa.

For those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there is an inquiry regarding the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*). For charioteers (*sūta*), village chiefs (*grāmaṇī*), attendants (*kṣattṛ*), and collectors (*saṃgrahītṛ*), the first [verse] is "From here, O Agni... Having churned the fire for them with this [verse], he should distribute the fires. With the verse, "May Jātavedas carry [thee] from thy own womb, knowing [the way]...", the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) is indeed [prescribed] for the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya... [and so on for the Vaiśya].

At that time, his Āhavanīya fire is the *āmātya*, the Gārhapatya fire is the *bhāgadugha*, and the Anvāhāryapacana fire is the *parivṛkti*. This is the deliberation regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). "They should bring the fire of birth-impurity (*sūtakāgni*)"—this is one view. "They should bring the *pradāyya* fire"—this is another view. [This is not in M.]

[K4 repeats once more: "They should bring that which is to be given"—this is one [view]; "they should bring that with which they burn the dead"—this is another [view, not in M]; "they should bring that with which women fashion their private parts"—this is yet another [view, M: *aikam*].
Having fetched fire from the house of a woman who has never given birth, they should kindle that single fire in the morning.

He offers a *caru* oblation for Bṛhaspati. In the house of the Brahman priest, he gives away a white-backed bull. The fuel-sticks are made of *pālāśa* wood. He recites: "This king, the slayer of Vṛtra... Having completed the offering, the Brahman priest, having become the king, says: "May he slay Vṛtra. Then, having returned, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Sutrāman. This sacrifice concludes in its own fires. They remain there.

In the morning, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra. In the house of a Rājanya, he gives a bull as a gift; the fuel-sticks are made of *nyagrodha* wood. He says: "May our king be a slayer of Vṛtra. Following the conclusion of the oblation, the chief queen and the Rājanya, having arrived, offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Aṃhomuc in their own fires.

This sacrifice concludes. They dwell there. In the morning, he offers a pap of cooked rice to Āditya. He gives a milch cow to the chief queen (*mahiṣī*) in her own house. For the sake of seizing fruit, the fuel consists of *badarī* wood. He says: "This king, the slayer of Vṛtra, comes to us. Following the conclusion of the oblation, [the queen] says: "May the chief queen kill the king. Having returned, this sacrifice is for Indra Sutrāman. They dwell there. In the morning, he offers a pap of cooked rice to Nirṛti.

For the sake of averting misfortune, having cooked in this single fire black rice (*vrīhi*) that has been split with the fingernails in the house, he performs a *darvihoma* sacrifice over the portions that have been spread with clarified butter and poured over them, using two verses addressed to Nirṛti: "O Goddess Nirṛti, what you have bound upon him, and whatever cruel thing was placed upon him—of that I offer a portion. He then gives black, bitter fruits to Aparṇā.

"The fuel-sticks are of *badarī* wood with dry tips; 'May he who is our king, the slayer of Vṛtra'—so he says. Having become the King after the completion of the oblation, the discarded wife (*parivṛktī*) should eat"—having said this, he returns and offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni at dawn for Indra Aṃhomuc. He gives gold in the house of the commander of the army. "The fuel-sticks are of *khadira* wood; 'May he who is our king, the slayer of Vṛtra'—so he says."

Following the conclusion of the oblation, the King, the commander of the army, having gone to Indra Sutrāman, offers a cake on eleven potsherds; at dawn, he offers a cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa. In the house of the charioteer, he gives a large castrated bull. The fuel is of *aśvattha* wood. He says: "He who is our King, the slayer of Vṛtra."

Following the conclusion of the oblation, the King, the son of the sacrifice, having gone to Indra Āhomuc, offers a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts at dawn. In the house of the village headman (*grāmaṇī*), he gives a speckled cow; the fuel is of *udumbara* wood. Having gone from this oblation to Indra Sutrāman, the King offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ at dawn. In the house of the chamberlain (*kṣattṛ*), he gives a speckled ox.

The fuel is of *plākṣa* wood. "This king of ours is the distributor of the oblation; let him go to Indra, the deliverer from distress. At dawn, he offers a cake on two potsherds to the Aśvins. He gives two cows that calve together to the charioteer (*saṃgrahītṛ*). The fuel is of two trees that grow together. "This king of ours is the distributor of the oblation; let him go to Indra, the good protector. At dawn, he offers a pap to Pūṣan. He gives a dark-colored bull to the tax-collector (*bhāgadugha*).

The sacrificial fuel consists of *kṣāmāpāka* wood; when the King, the distributor of our oblation, has gone to Indra Aṃhomuc, he offers a *gāvīdhuka* pap for Rudra at dawn. In the house of the Akṣāvāpa, he gives away a brindled bull that has been castrated. The sacrificial fuel consists of *rauhiṣa* wood; when the Akṣāvāpa, the King, has gone to our oblation, he offers back a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Sutraman in his own fires. This sacrifice concludes. These are the days.

At that time, he himself milks a white cow with a white calf; he himself curdles it, they themselves churn it, and having stripped off a branch of the *aśvattha* tree, he fashions a four-cornered cup. He says, "We must set aside the milk of this [cow]. They remain [there].

In the morning, he pours out the oblation for Mitra and Bṛhaspati, prepared with the milk of a white cow that has a white calf, and which has been heated by itself. With the [mixture] for Mitra, he mixes the [curds] for Bṛhaspati. At the very hearing of this [formula], the portion for Mitra is indeed the vessel, while the portion for Bṛhaspati is the stirring-ladle. He proceeds first with the [oblation] for Bṛhaspati.

The altar is prepared by Maitra-Uttara himself; the sacrificial grass is spread by him himself, the fuel is prepared by him himself. He gives this very white cow with a white calf as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This is the enumeration of the years from that point; indeed, having sacrificed with these two oblations for the sake of the gods, from that time on it is so.

Having sacrificed with the *dava*, he performs sacrifices for four months with those same two oblations; he attains the early summer (*graīṣma*). He sacrifices with the *varuṇapraghāsas*; having sacrificed with them, he performs sacrifices for four months with these same two oblations; he attains the rainy season (*vārṣika*). With the *sākamedhas*... all... he attains.
[18] "Āṃ, all... [6] ...he attains. He performs the *Śunāsīrīya* sacrifice.

Having sacrificed with those two oblations, he sacrifices throughout the entire month of Mārgaśīrṣa with these very same oblations. And for twenty-five nights of the month of Taiṣya, [there is] the *Indraturīya*: one *Indraturīya*, one [offering] with five fuel-sticks, one *Devikā* oblation, two [offerings] of the *Triṣaṃyukta* [sacrifices], and one [offering] of the *Vaiśvānaravāruṇa*... of those [sacrifices] that have been prescribed.

And there are twelve oblations for the Ratnins [two for him... for Vaiśvānara, for Varuṇa... ten oblations for the Ratnins]; thus his sacrifice takes place during the dark fortnight of Māgha. Then his sacrifice is performed with ten oblations of bark from trees that have been felled by fire over five days.

Soma remains in those [residues]; they stay there. In the morning he undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*). They stay [there]. In the morning he purchases the King (Soma). Having purchased him, they carry him—bound with a tiger skin—to the house of the Brahman priest. For the other [priests], he prepares the guest-offering (*ātithya*) in the established manner. They bring him [back] during this three-day period at the time for his swelling (*āpyāyana*).

The rite of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma is accomplished; following the cake-offering for the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, he offers the oblations of the Devasū offerings together with that cake-offering.

"To Agni Gṛhapati... [K4,70a4] ...he recites these eight [verses]. For the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), there is the formal call (*praiṣa*): "Recite the invitatory verse; sacrifice! For the other oblations, it is whispered (*upāṃśu*). The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has the same call, and the *iḍā* portion is shared. When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he says to him: "May Savitṛ impel you for the impellings. [He continues]: "Agni of the householders... of the lords of dharma," and with the verse, "O gods who are the impellers of the gods," he takes his right hand.

He takes hold [of him], saying: "This one, the son of such-and-such, is the king of the non-Brāhmaṇas. With the two verses, "Against this the name of kingship has been established," and "His own body has extended itself," he wipes his face with clarified butter. Having stepped out the Viṣṇu-strides, saying, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu; thou art the wide-stride of Viṣṇu," they dwell there.

The rites are accomplished with the morning-pressing *puroḍāśa* cakes; the cake for the Maruts on twenty-one potsherds is prescribed. Regarding its potsherds, he arranges them with the two sets of formulas beginning "This one" (*imaṃ*) and "Bright-light" (*śukrajyotis*); he places the set to be recited in the forest (*araṇye-anuvākyam*) on both sides, and the central set in the middle. Then those waters, having been drawn along with their vessels, remain for him.

In the waters that are seasonal, having flowed thus toward the dawn, the Pratiprasthātṛ first digs wells following the current; those waters are the *uvekā*s. He distresses one, leads away another, and deposits another. The Adhvaryu goes to half of the waters with four spoonfuls of ghee in a well-known manner.

They go bringing the abundant clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī* and they draw up the *sruva*-ladle. They take the *nigrābhyā* waters, the *ekadhana* jars, and the *pānnejana* waters. The *adhvaryu* takes four portions of butter with the *pracaraṇī* ladle and he offers it.

"Ye are purposeful; ye are givers of sovereignty; give sovereignty, svāhā!"—thus over the flowing waters. "Ye are givers of sovereignty; give sovereignty to so-and-so"—thus he draws it up with the *naumaṇḍa* vessel. "Thou art the lord of waters; thou art a giver of sovereignty; give sovereignty, svāhā"—thus he offers the oblation while the waters are being poured around the lord of waters. "Thou art a giver of sovereignty; give sovereignty to so-and-so"—thus he draws it up. "Whatever wood is there..."

They take [the milk] from it with a vessel: "Thou art the wave of the rain-god (*ūrmi*); thou art the giver of sovereignty (*rāṣṭradā*); grant sovereignty, svāhā!"—thus he offers into the *ūrmyā* waters. "Thou art the giver of sovereignty; grant sovereignty to so-and-so"—thus he draws [the remainder].

Whatever wood they take there, from that he offers with a vessel: "Thou art the host of the rain-god (*vṛṣasena*); thou art the giver of sovereignty; grant sovereignty, svāhā!"—thus he offers while the *vārṣasenī* waters are flowing. "Thou art the giver of sovereignty; grant sovereignty to so-and-so"—thus he draws [the remainder].

Whatever wood they take from there, with a vessel made of that he offers an oblation with the formula: "You are firmly established; you are the givers of the kingdom; give the kingdom, svāhā!"—thus he offers over the *kūpyā* waters. With the cover of the well, he draws up water with the formula: "You are the givers of the kingdom; give the kingdom to so-and-so. He offers an oblation over the *dhruvakṣita* waters with the formula: "You are the strength of the Maruts; you are the givers of the kingdom; give the kingdom, svāhā!"—[the formula continues: "You are the givers of the kingdom; the kingdom..."

"Give this to such-and-such"—with these words he draws up [the milk] from a vessel made of a tree struck by lightning. He offers it with the formula: "You are sun-bright; you are givers of the kingdom; give the kingdom, svāhā!"—thus he offers over the *paridṛśni* plants with the formula: "You are givers of the kingdom; the kingdom..."

"Give this to so-and-so"—thus he draws it up with the *śukra* cup, saying, "You are of sun-like skin; you are givers of sovereignty; give sovereignty, svāhā! He offers it while the rain falls in warm drops. "You are givers of sovereignty; give sovereignty to so-and-so"—thus he draws it up with the bronze vessel (*kāṃsasthāla*), saying, "You are gentle; you are givers of sovereignty; give sovereignty, svāhā! He offers it while the rain falls in loud claps.

"You are givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty to this person"—with these words he draws [the water] with the bowl of *varaṇa* wood. "You are the willing; grant sovereignty, svāhā!"—with these words he offers [the oblation] into the stationary [fires]. "You are givers of sovereignty... [he repeats].

"Give the kingdom to so-and-so," he says as he lifts it up with a vessel made of *nyagrodha* wood; he offers it with the formula: "You are the powerful ones (*śakvarī*), you are the givers of the kingdom; give the kingdom, svāhā! He offers over the *daivyāḥ* verses [with the formula]: "You are the givers of the kingdom... [The following underlined passage is not found in K4].

With the *camasa* [ladle], he offers into the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the formula: “You are the splendor of Agni; you are the givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty, svāhā! Then, drawing out [the butter] from the *ājyasthālī* [butter-pot], he offers into the water and the plants with the formula: “You are the essence; you are the givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty, svāhā! With the *gṛṣṭibandhana* [cord used for tying a first-calf cow], he offers into the milk with the formula: “You are the sustainers of all; you are the givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty, svāhā! [He offers] into the milk with the *godohana* [milk-pail] with the formula: “You are the givers of sovereignty... (The rest of the formula follows).

[19] With the milk-pail, he offers, saying: "You are the supporters of people; you are the givers of the kingdom; give the kingdom, svāhā! He places [the remainder] in curd, saying: "You are the givers of the kingdom; give the kingdom to so-and-so," and he draws it up with the cup, saying: "You are the splendor of Agni..."

(16) With the formula, "Ye are the splendor of Agni; ye are the givers of sovereignty; grant us sovereignty, svāhā! he offers into the clarified butter from the *camasa*. Then, drawing [the butter] up from the *ājyasthālī* with the formula, "Ye are the givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty to so-and-so," [he says]: "Ye are the essence of the waters and the plants; ye are the givers of sovereignty; grant us sovereignty, svāhā! Thus he offers.

He offers [the oblation] with the formula: "O honeyed ones, you are the givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty to such-and-such a person. He draws up [the water] with a vessel from a tree in which they find honey. He offers [the oblation] with the formula: "O divine waters, you are honeyed, free from enemies, and givers of sovereignty; grant sovereignty, svāhā! At the Sārasvata offerings, he draws up [the water] with the formula: "O givers of sovereignty, grant sovereignty to such-and-such a person. <10.5>

They proceed with a four-cornered vessel made of *udumbara* wood. When the Adhvaryu pours out the *vasatīvarī* waters at the edge of the *catvāla*, the Pratiprasthātṛ performs this rite over the common water-vessel (*sata*) with the formula: "O divine waters, you who are full of sweetness, be united with these sweet waters; you who possess great splendor, being praised for the sake of the Kṣatriya. They step forward with the *nigrābhya* waters by the eastern path, and they stand by the western path with the *vasatīvarī* waters and the *ekadhana* waters. These waters are well-known.
Having thus offered the remnants as a libation, performed the Ukthya sacrifice, and entered [the sacrificial hall], the Adhvaryu offers the Dadhigraha belonging to Prajāpati.

Then, with the formula, “May these waters, unassailable, sit down, full of vigor,” he places them between the *dhiṣṇiya* of the Hotṛ and that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, saying, “Bestowing great splendor upon the Kṣatriya. Having placed four *vāyavya* cups among them, he hastens forward, holding a golden pair of tongs and a *śatamāna* weight, while pouring out the third portion of the *vasatīvarī* waters with the formula, “May Agni protect us at the morning pressing.”

They bring that Ekadhana vessel to the other jar; the pressing is straightforward and well-established, and the cups are drawn from the Āgrayaṇa vessel. Having taken the Āgrayaṇa cup and touched water, he moves forward along the eastern side with the formula, "Thou art unassailable, the bond of speech. With a golden pair of tongs, he takes up a *śatamāna* weight of gold with the formula, "Born of heat, thou art the gift of Soma. With the formula, "I purify the bright ones with the bright," he purifies these waters with this [vessel]: "The radiant ones with the radiant, the immortal ones..."

With the verse addressed to Varuṇa, "O you who are praised together, these brilliant ones are for strength," he draws [the draught] with the verse beginning, "Unassailable waters, you have been brought hither; within them [is the draught]; you are taken with a base; I take you, acceptable to Sarasvatī. Having drawn it with a *palāśa* leaf, he places it in front of the *sata*. With the formula, "This is your womb; for Sarasvatī, you," he does the same after having drawn it with a *naiyyagrodha* leaf.

He places it to the south; in the same manner, having taken it with an *aśvattha* branch, he places it to the west; in the same manner, having taken it with an *udumbara* branch, he places it to the north.

Having touched water, he runs around by the east, draws the *ukthya* cup, and draws the *dhruva* cup. The rite is completed; together with the *puroḍāśa* cakes for the morning pressing, he sets down the cake on twenty-one potsherds for the Maruts.

Having offered the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) belonging to the morning pressing, he says: "Recite the invitatory prayer for the Maruts. There should be a portion spread with butter and sprinkled over it for the Maruts; the Hotṛ alone recites the subsequent formula for this, and the Hotṛ performs the offering. He says, "O Śrauṣaṭ," and "Recite the offering prayer for the Maruts. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation. They carry one cake of the Maruts forward to the Āgnīdhra before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has been made. Thus the morning pressing is successfully completed.

They sit down for the midday pressing; when the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down, the sacrificer puts on a garment of *tārpya* silk with the formula, "Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra. He wraps his turban around with the formula, "The source of the Kṣatra. At this time, they cause the wife to put on [the garment]. He brings down the chariot with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; through thee may he slay Vṛtra."

With the words, "Thus, by the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the directors, I yoke thee," he yokes the chariot drawn by side-horses to the north of the Āgnīdhra fire-shed. Having gone around to the north of the Āgnīdhra, he offers the oblations. He leads the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) southward.

Having led the sacrificial gifts, they enter the Āgnīdhra shed. There, with the formula, "May Citpati purify thee; may Vācpati purify thee," he purifies him with one hundred and one tufts of *darbha* grass. He causes him to eat curd, he causes him to eat *udumbara* fruit, he causes him to eat young grass shoots, and [he gives him] wool.

Saying, "Agni is the lord of the house," he causes him to recite the *āvida* formulas while leading him forward; saying, "Indra is the king of the aged Brahmins," [he leads him] by the front of the *havirdhāna* shed with the formula, "Thou art the splendor of Soma. [He leads him] to the *āhavanīya* fire within the *havirdhāna* sheds...

He spreads a tiger skin over the *āhavanīya* fire with its neck facing east and the hair upwards, saying: "May my splendor be like thine; thou art immortality. Having touched the gold plate (*rukmam*) with the words, "Protect me from death," and having made a lap, he sits down facing east. With the words, "Protect me from the lightning-flash," he places the golden plate above him. With the words, "May the biting serpents be driven away," he pierces a eunuch with lead through the mouth. With the words, "The head of Namuci is cast out," he [pierces] the right...

... (6) he discards [the grass-blade] with the words, "Mount the fuel-stick," and causes these two to mount. ... (15) he discards [it]... "Mount"—thus he causes him to mount the diś... [10] he causes him to mount; he rises up after [the fire], he strides along mentally, and offers six oblations to the quarters (*pārthāni*). There are six offerings for the subjugation of the elements (*bhūtānām aveṣṭi*). With the words, "Soma is King," he causes him to recite this before the consecration (*praṇābhiṣeka*). [EM] [M: //]
"May Varuṇa and those gods who are the impellers of dharma cause his speech to flow," he says of him... "may they cause him to flow. He says of him: "...may they cause him to flow."

[8] He says, “May they swell for you. He says to him, “May they swell for you as your eye. He says to him, “May they swell for you as your ear. He says, “May they swell for you as your ear. With the words, “I consecrate you with the splendor of Soma,” the Adhvaryu first sprinkles him from the front with a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood; likewise from the south with one made of *aśvattha* wood, and so on for the Rājanya.

[The Adhvaryu] sprinkles him from the east with an Udumbara branch in this very manner; the other [priest], the Adhvaryu, sprinkles him from the front in this very manner. [The Brahman] sprinkles him from the south with a Nyagrodha branch in this very manner; [the Hotṛ] sprinkles him from the west with an Aśvattha branch in this very manner; and [the Adhvaryu] sprinkles him from the north with an Udumbara branch in this very manner.

[The Udgātṛ priest says: "O Agni, protect from heaven... Having turned back, he does not hold [the vessel] low. [He says: "Turned toward the north," and thus he strokes the hair with strides. With the verse, "Following the one dwelling in the depths, she who goes to her sisters," he offers exactly six oblations to the quarters (*pārthāni*). Having poured together the remnants in a single vessel, [he addresses] Rudra...

Having gone northward with the words, "That which is thy highest name, O Purchaser," he offers it in the Āgnīdhra fire with the formula, "To him it has been offered; may I be that, svāhā! Having placed in the ladle or the cup that which remains there with the words, "That which exists," he recites, "O Prajāpati, none other than thou possesses these."

Having gone toward the west, he offers in the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: "All beings... of riches, svāhā! If he should desire of his wife, "May her offspring be sovereign," she should touch him from behind; thus her offspring indeed becomes sovereign.

With the words, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he approaches the chariot with the Viṣṇu-strides; having arrived, with the words, "Thou art the stridden of Viṣṇu," and then with the words, "Thou art the wrath of cattle," he puts on the boar-skin sandals, thinking, "May my wrath be like thine. With the words, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra," the Adhvaryu hands him a bow, [thinking], "By thee may he [slay] Vṛtra..."

"May you slay," [he says]; "for the subduing of enemies. "And pierce the enemies with arrows, like a well-aimed shaft at its mark"—with these words he seeks out the quarters; "protect us from the destructive powers, directed across"—[he says]. "O golden-hued ones, in the radiance of the dawns"—with this *triṣṭubh* verse he raises his arms. "Like two pillars risen at the rising of the sun, ascend the seat of Mitra and Varuṇa."

Having thus paid homage, he mounts the chariot. Then, with the verse, "Behold Aditi and Diti," and with the words, "They have grasped the right hand of Indra," the Pratiprasthātṛ, using a *triṣṭubh* verse addressed to Indra, mounts after him.

"Desiring wealth, like those seeking wealth, O Indra... With these three hundred verses, the kṣatriya, having been instructed, comes to rest in the eastern quarter. Saying, "May I conquer at the impulse of the Maruts," he sets forth. Having reached his destination, he asks, "Whose cows are these? "Such-and-such's," [he replies]. "My mind has attained them," [he says], and thus he conquers. "Together with power and vigor," he says, and returns, coming back again.

While the wives stand at the edge of the *cātvāla* pit, the sacrificer, without even standing still, draws a bow across them from side to side while reciting, "Thou art delight; thou art pleasure," and he causes [the bowstring] to be fixed with the words, "Thou art noble."

[He stands] on the earth with the mantra, "Homage to the mother; may she not harm me, may the wind not harm me. Then they bring him a stone, which he fastens on with the mantra, "So much is your life; bestow life upon me"—a golden one with the mantra, "You are vigor; bestow vigor upon me"—and an udumbara one with the mantra, "You are union; you are luster; bestow luster upon me"—and yet another golden one with the mantra, "To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā! These are the *rathavimocanīya* verses.

He offers with the formula: "To Śoma Vanaspati, svāhā! To the impeller, svāhā! When these have been offered, they unharness the chariot; therefore it does not stop there. Having grasped the reins... [K4:71b1]

With the formula, "The gatherer, seated upon the pure," he places the chariot upon the chariot-stand together with the driver; he places it to the east of the chariot-pole and between the two shafts of the chariot-stand. The driver crawls underneath it. He gives these leather straps and the chariot to the Brahman priest. They bring the curd-mixture for Mitra-Varuṇa which has been set out, and the cake on twenty-one potsherds for the Maruts; over that [cake], [he recites] "May Mitra be..."

Having cleansed his right hand, the sacrificer places [the earth]; with the words, "Thou art Varuṇa," he places the northern one; with the words, "May I be peaceful through all the gods," he mixes them together, saying, "That [peace] through me..."

With the verse, “O Viśve Devas,” he proceeds with that offering. Together with the *sviṣṭakṛt* of that [offering], he offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* of the Maruts. Having performed the *iḍā*-portioning in common for both, having proceeded with this [offering], he places the Audumbara throne-seat to the south of the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, “Thou art the navel of the Kṣatra. With the formula, “Thou art the womb of the Kṣatra,” he spreads a coverlet upon it. The sacrificer mounts it and sits down upon it, turning toward the east, having made a lap. <10.7> [K4,71a13–; M339–]

He says to him, "Sit on what is pleasant"; he replies, "I have sat on what is pleasant. He says to him, "Sit on what is well-seated"; he replies, "I have sat on what is well-seated. He says to him, "May it not harm you"; he replies, "May it not harm me."

He worships the one who has sat down with the verse, “He of firm vows has sat down” (*niṣasāda dhṛtavrata*). With the words, “Varuṇa, the wise one, for the sovereignty of his own wives,” he addresses the Brahman priest with the word “Brahman. He says to him, “O King, you are the Brahman,” and “You are Savitṛ of true impulse. With the word “Brahman,” he addresses the Adhvaryu; he says to him, “O King, you are the Brahman,” and “You are Indra of true power. With the word “Brahman,” [he addresses the next].

To the *hotṛ*, he says, "O King, you are the *brahman*," and "You are Mitra, the most gracious. To the *udgātṛ*, he says, "O King, you are the *brahman*," and "You are Varuṇa, whose law is truth. To this [officiant], he bestows the wealth of Indra and his steadfastness.

"He gives it to the *tamas* among the *kṣatra*; by that, may he be won over for me"—thus he consecrates [the dice], saying: "To the *kṣatra*, to the charioteer; to the charioteer, to the tax-collector; to the tax-collector, to the keeper of the dice; by that, may he be won over for me; may he not be won over against me; may he be fit for sacrifice for me"—thus [K4, M: *tena medhya tena me radhya*]. With that, having thrown [the dice], the keeper of the dice [speaks].

Below that, he digs out the gaming-ground (*adhidevana*) for the chariot-stand (*rathavāhana*). He sprinkles it with salt water, covers it with mud, and pours five hundred dice made of gold upon it. While the rice-porridge cooked in ghee is being prepared, he recites: "We proclaim [the game]."

Thus they say: "The possessors of jewels sit around the gaming board; then there is a hollow in the rice-pot. Taking up five dice, the Adhvaryu throws them, saying: 'This is the King's opening, the unconquerable. As they win, they take [the stakes]; they sacrifice around the Akṣāvāpa; having won the highest prize, they conquer the quarters."

Saying, "Thou art a king," the Adhvaryu hands five dice to the sacrificer; saying, "A fair song," he addresses the Kṣattṛ, and says to him, "O King, thou art one of fair song"; saying, "Of auspicious fortune," he addresses the Saṃgrahītṛ, and says to him, "O King, thou art one of auspicious fortune"; saying, "A true king," he addresses the Bhāgadugha, and says to him, "O King, thou art a true king."

Regarding the "truthful laws" (*satyadharmān*), the dice-player says to him, "O King, you are the truthful law. They take those very dice from him with the formula, "For cultivation thee! and "For security thee! With the former [formula], he places them in the pit of the *sadas*. He causes the story of Śunaḥśepa to be told; he causes the story of the golden cushion (*hiraṇyakaśipu*) to be told; he causes the story of the golden cushion to be told.

There are more than a hundred [gold pieces]. Seated upon a golden cushion (*hiraṇyakaśipu*), the Hotṛ recites the *śastra*; standing upon a golden mat (*hiraṇyakūrca*), the Adhvaryu responds with the *pratihāra*. His response is this very one: "Oṃ, Hotṛ! So be it, O Hotṛ! And he gives fifty and a hundred cows to the Hotṛ upon that golden cushion.

These two golden bowls and five hundred cows are for the *adhvaryu*. Those cows which they bring when they defeat a *rājanya*—this fat, butter-filled bull—they take for themselves with the formulas, "For plowing thee" and "For security thee. They place it to the east of the *sadas* shed with the formula, "Recite for Indra accompanied by the Maruts," and the rest is well known.

He proceeds with three Marutvatīya offerings. He descends for the consumption of the Marutvatīya cup with the formula, "O Sovereign! The midday pressing is successfully completed. The third pressing is successfully completed. Regarding the whey on the enclosing sticks, his consumption formula is: "That seed of yours which is poured out—that I consume. The ritual action is successfully completed up to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).

With the formula, “To Apānnaptr, svāhā! he offers a spoonful (sruvāhuti) into the waters while rising from the *avabhṛtha* bath. With the formula, “To Ūrjānnaptr, svāhā! having emerged, he offers it into a clump of *darbha* grass. With the formula, “To Agni Gṛhapati, svāhā! he returns and offers it into the *gārhapatya* fire. The rite is accomplished; it concludes.

This is the twenty-first Ukthya, the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice. The Pavamāna stotra consists of thirty-four verses. There is a barren cow for Heaven and Earth; the sacrificial cake for the animal offering belongs to Heaven and Earth and is prepared on a single potsherd. Having proceeded with the two omenta, he turns back.
Indeed, these three halls are measured out. To the south of the middle hall...

There are six [days] of the Uddhata sacrifice. Within the sacrificial hall itself, on the seventh day at the very end, they conclude the Uddhata sacrifice and dwell there. In the morning, he offers a pap (caru) to Sarasvatī. He gives young bulls as gifts. He places a white lotus (puṇḍarīka) in a water-pitcher. This sacrifice is completed. Having gathered together, they dwell there. In the morning, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ. He gives a soiled bull as a gift.

He places a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) in the water-jar. This sacrifice is concluded. Having come together, they dwell [there]. In the morning, he offers a pap (*caru*) for Pūṣan; he gives a dark-colored animal; [he places it] in the water-jar—in the morning.

He offers a *caru* oblation to Bṛhaspati; he gives a spotted bull as the sacrificial fee. In the morning, at the water-vessel, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra; he gives a bull as the sacrificial fee. In the morning, at the water-vessel, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Varuṇa; he gives a large castrated bull as the sacrificial fee. He places a lotus flower in the water-vessel. This sacrifice concludes right there.

They dwell in the hall on the seventh day. In the morning, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Tvaṣṭṛ; he gives a *śuṇṭha* as the sacrificial gift. This sacrifice is completed. Following the conclusion of this, the Adhvaryu fastens a garland of seven lotuses onto the sacrificer. He puts it on him.

Having prepared that very initiation and the sacrificial implements, and having carried forward the waters, he offers the introductory oblation (*prāyaṇīya*). Having offered the *samiṣṭayajus* with the mantra, "Thou art its heat," he either gives the *śāṇḍīvala* weaned calves to the Soma-seller. They bring this King [Soma], covered with a tiger skin, from the house of the Brahman priest.

For him, he offers the well-established guest-offering (*ātithya*). The rite is successfully established at the first *upasad*. At the morning performance, the cake on eight potsherds for Agni is cooked; in the vessel dedicated to Agni, he takes the portion of the cake for Agni, which has been spread with clarified butter and sprinkled over. With that, he offers it as a continuous oblation. Gold is its sacrificial fee. At the morning performances, they are offered during the middle *upasad*.

The *caru* for Soma is cooked; the vessel for Agni is [prepared]. In the vessel for Soma, he takes the food for the middle [portion]; in the vessel for Soma, he takes the Soma-offering with the under-layered and over-sprinkled butter. With that, he offers it. A tawny-colored animal is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the final *upasad*. At the morning performance, the three-potherd offering for Viṣṇu is cooked.
Having offered the vessels for Agni and Soma, [he proceeds].

In the Vaiṣṇava [offering], he offers the [oblation] into the vessel; this is his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). He offers together with that; these are his sacrificial fees. This is the *agniṣṭoma*, the seventeen-fold *daśapeya*. He for whom there are ten paternal grandmothers who are Brahman-widows and ten maternal grandmothers—those are his officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); he for whom there are five [such] paternal grandmothers...

The five maternal grandmothers of the *brahmabandhu* are such as have been mentioned; a hundred [of them] drink the *brāhma*... for the *adhvaryu*... the seventeenfold *stotra* occurs; the two mirrors are for the *adhvaryu*...

A Bhārgava, unyoked from his cart, becomes the Agnīdh’s assistant; the Hotṛ priest belongs to the lineage of Bhṛgu. At the midday pressing, they praise the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin with the Śrāyantīya chant. They perform the Vāravantīya as the Agniṣṭoma-sāman and the Yajñāyajñīya. He draws the Sarasvatī waters. As for the Vasatīvarī waters, [they are used] for the *trigraha*... [the *nigrābhya* waters... for the *nigrābhyā*.

All those water-offerings become dedicated to Sarasvatī. This Agniṣṭoma sacrifice concludes as a seventeen-fold Daśapeya. A barren cow for Ka is to be immolated; after performing the ritual with the omenta of the two cows, he offers a cake on one potsherd to Kāya and then turns back.
Thus:

<10.10> Having dwelt [there], they perform the *diśām aveṣṭi* sacrifices in the morning. He offers a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, a pap for the Viśve Devas, curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa, and a pap for Bṛhaspati.

The sacrificial fee for this [offering] consists of gold, a reddish-brown bull, and a four-year-old cow that is barren. Following the continuity of the lineage, he offers the oblation for the Hotṛ priest. The rite is successfully accomplished; it is concluded. This is the iṣṭi.

While they are dwelling, let them remain; this is the sacrifice while they dwell. In the morning, he immolates a pregnant ewe for Āditya and a spotted, four-year-old cow that is pregnant for Marut. The one for Āditya is pregnant, while the one for Marut is not pregnant. He proceeds first with the offering for Āditya and then with the one for Marut. He causes the announcement (*āśrāvayati*) loudly for the offering to Āditya, but in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) for the one for Marut. These two animal sacrifices are concluded.

They dwell there until morning. At dawn, he buys young shoots from a eunuch for a lead weight. With woolen fringes, he purchases rice from a potter. He offers a cake on twelve potsherds to the Aśvins and Pūṣan. Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*), they cook a mess of this rice on the Anvāhāryapacana fire. When it has cooled, they cover it with stones that have been struck.

With the mantra, “The sweet ones with the sweet,” he mixes them; with the mantra, “The strong ones with the strong, the nectar with the nectar, I unite with Soma,” they enclose the water-pot to the west of that very *anvāhāryapacana* fire. Having formed three lumps, he places them down; having gathered them together, he addresses them with the mantra, “Soma art thou, Soma art thou.”

When the *prāśitra* has been set aside for him, he uncovers it and looks at it, saying, "Cook for the Aśvins. He offers the oblation to the Hotṛ continuously. The rite is successfully accomplished; this sacrifice is concluded. In the morning, they remain there and he offers a pap (*caru*) to Sarasvatī of true speech, and a cake on twelve potsherds (*puroḍāśa*) to Savitṛ of true impulsion.

Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he should dispatch messengers of truth (*satyadūta*) to the districts, commanding them: "This man, the son of such-and-such, has died. If anyone does not descend from him as a messenger, his head shall split apart.

If someone were to rise up against him, he should approach that person. When the *prāśitra* has been set aside, he looks at it after uncovering it, saying: "O Sarasvatī of true speech (*satyavāc*), cook! This sacrifice follows the continuity [of the previous one]. They stay overnight; in the morning, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Sutrāman. When the *prāśitra* of that [offering] has been set aside, he looks at it after uncovering it, saying: "O [ghee], cook for Indra Sutrāman!"
The *anuṣeṣṭi* offerings are performed for the continuity [of the lineage]; they are performed in the morning. Thus [ends the section on the *ṣautrāmaṇī*].
Therefore, for that [sacrifice], the materials for the Sautrāmaṇī are:

lion hair and *kvala*-barley flour; tiger hair and jujube flour; wolf hair and wild jujube flour; three *upayāma* vessels; four *vāyavya* cups; a *vāra* vessel and a *sata* vessel; a *śatātṛṇṇā* vessel and a *śatamāna* weight; a mare and a sacrificial post; a cup for the Aśvins; a smoky-colored goat for Sarasvatī; a ram for Indra; and a bull for Bṛhaspati.
One who has failed in his vows, or whose soma has been over-purified, or who has vomited soma, should sacrifice this [bull].
First, he should offer the most excellent Soma of the *atipavitra* (exceedingly purified) variety; he should not disregard this, for it is the unimpaired [sacrifice].

If he were to perform this [rite], he should prepare a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) as the animal-offering-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) for him, and by means of that he should proceed in its proper place.

If he sacrifices right here where his fires are located, having given to the ancestors on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, he prepares the altar to the east of the *āhavanīya* fire, leaving space for a chariot.

If they conclude the sacrifice or depart, having offered to the ancestors with the *āgnīdhrīya* fires, he prepares the altar to the east of the *āhavanīya* fire, leaving space for a chariot. At the same time that the *adhvaryu* prepares the altar, the *pratiprasthātṛ* digs out a pit to the south of the *āgnīdhrīya* fire. At the same time that the *adhvaryu* prepares the *uttaravedi*, the *pratiprasthātṛ* pours sand into the pit.

At the time when the Adhvaryu is about to place the fire, at the very moment when he throws the fuel onto the Āhavanīya fire, the Pratiprasthātṛ brings fire from the Anvāhāryapacana fire, scatters it upon the sand in the pit (akhara), and kindles it.

At the time when the Adhvaryu takes the portions of clarified butter along with the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), at that same time the Pratiprasthātṛ purifies the surā with a sieve using the mantra: "May the flowing stream purify thee" (TS 1.8.21b), ending with "the soma of Sūrya, with his eternal lineage."
With the verse, "The wind is purified by the filter" (ŚB 1.8.21.1c1), one should not purify [the Soma], for this [verse] is deficient;

rather, one should purify with it only when it has been over-purified. Or, as it says, "Soma flows backward for one who vomits Soma" (ibid. c2); one should address one who has over-purified [the Soma] with this, saying "backward," whereas for one who has not over-purified, one should say "forward" (cf. ŚB 2.6.1.2).
One should not pay heed to one who has vomited Soma, for he is deprived of this [efficacy].
He sprinkles the fuel and the sacrificial grass, he sprinkles the altar, and he sprinkles what has been placed near.

Having poured out water, he takes the *prastara* bundle; he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); having stepped forward toward the east, he lays down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) made of *kārṣmarya* wood;
he places two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) upon the fire.
Having caused [the sacrificer] to recite over the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he yokes the fire;
having approached, he places the *tiraścī* [stick];
upon the two *tiraścī* sticks he places the *prastara* [bunch of grass], upon the *prastara* the *juhū* [ladle], and the other two *barhis* [blades of grass].
Having approached, he says, “The firm ones have settled”; having touched them together with the formula, “That which for me, O Agni...,” he recites the *Daśahotṛ* formula.

Having touched water and taken one of these cups dedicated to Vāyu, he draws the *Dadhigraha* belonging to Prajāpati with the formula, “At thy will they all turn toward thee” (3.5.10.1a–b1), and “When thou hast fought twice with these... [up to] “Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati.
He places it so that it does not touch the previous ladle (*sruk*) with the formula, “This is thy womb; for Prajāpati, thee” (3.5.10.1b2).
Having touched water, he runs forward along the east;

then he draws these cups with the *upayāma* formulas: "Have they not indeed come? "Thou art taken with a base; I take thee, acceptable to the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman. This is thy womb; thee for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman.
Thus he deposits them and mixes them with groats and wool.

With the verse, “*kuvid aṅga*,” he draws [the draught], saying: “Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Sarasvatī, to Indra the Good Protector, and to the Aśvins. This is thy womb: for Sarasvatī, for Indra the Good Protector, and for the Aśvins. He places it down. He mixes it with groats and wool.
Having sprinkled the sacrificial post, raised it, and encircled it with the rope, they immolate these animals upon it: a smoky-grey horse for the Aśvins, a ram for Sarasvatī, and a bull for Indra.
Having offered their omenta and performed the purification, he takes this curd-offering for Prajāpati and offers it, saying: "To Prajāpati, svāhā!"
He grants a boon to him;
having set down the vessel in its proper place and touched water, he runs around by the east,
while the Brahman and the sacrificer sit down to the south.
The Hotṛ moves forward.
The Adhvaryu takes two Vāyu cups, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes one.
"Recite for the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman"—thus he says. While pouring these draughts into the vessels dedicated to Vāyu, he recites, "O Aśvins, you two [drank] the surā-mixture.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice to the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra Sutrāman."
"Like parents [worship] their son, so both Aśvins [worship]," he sacrifices;
"Recite for Agni," he says, while pouring the remnants together into a single vessel; "O Agni, thou art to be offered," he recites.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni.
He sacrifices with the verse, "In whom horses, bulls, and oxen [dwell]," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.
They bring these two residues for him: that of the *dadhighraha* and that of the *surāgraha*.
He awaits them with the mantra: "For separate indeed are the two seats ordained by the gods, measured out in the highest heaven; do not let them mingle in the supreme firmament" (TB 1.4.2.2).
With the words, "Thou art the intoxicating *surā*" (TB 1.4.2.2), the Brāhmaṇa avoids the *surāgraha*.
"This is Soma," with these words he takes up the cup of curds; "Thou art spirituous liquor, thou art intoxicating," with these words the Kṣatriya takes up the cup of *surā*;
"This is Soma," with these words he wipes the cup of curds.

"Do not harm me, entering your own womb," with these words the Brāhmaṇa consumes the *dadhigraha* cup; and "Do not harm me, entering your own womb," with these words the Rājanya consumes the *surāgraha* cup. If a Rājanya should sacrifice, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should consume this *dadhigraha* cup by calling out to one another, [reciting]: "Of that which remains here of the pressed juice..."
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, he should hire a Brāhmaṇa as the drinker of the remnant of the oblation of *surā*;
"If he should not find a Brāhmaṇa, he should pour it into an anthill" (TB 1.8.6.2)— thus indeed he pours it into an anthill,
having tied a sling to a long bamboo pole.
They fix two pillars on both sides of the southern fire;
they set a crossbeam across them, either supporting it or simply laying it down;
upon that, they lay this Śatātṛṇṇā brick.
He ties a *śatamāna* coin beneath it;
having fastened a *śatamāna* coin, he places it where they hold the hundred blades of grass.
Then, with three verses addressed to Vāyu, they proceed together to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), [reciting]: "I have heard of two paths, the sign... (TB 1.4.2.3).
"O God Varuṇa, that bond of yours which has the *gāyatrī* meter—by this, O Vāyavya, I release it," he says for the first time;
"O God Varuṇa, that bond of yours which has the *triṣṭubh* meter—by this, I release it," he says for the second time;
"O God Varuṇa, that bond of yours which has the *jagatī* meter—by this, I release it," he says for the third time.

Having arrived, he worships the ancestors with the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses. The Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ, and the Brahman [worship] with three *śatātṛṇṇā* verses for the Soma that has been unsuccessful or has overflowed. [He offers] a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, one on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, and one on ten potsherds for Varuṇa.
Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he proceeds with the animal sacrifices ending with the *iḍā*.
He proceeds with the sacrificial cakes accompanied by the *iḍā* formula;
he proceeds with the sacrificial cakes prior to the after-offerings (*anūyāja*); thus it concludes. 4. The [cakes] are completed.

In the morning, he offers the oblations of the Prayuj sacrifices: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, a pap for Bṛhaspati, and a cake on eight potsherds for Tvaṣṭṛ;
he gives away the southern pole of the chariot as the sacrificial fee; this sacrifice is concluded.
They dwell [there].

In the morning, he offers the oblations for the *atiyuj* (horses). He prepares a *caru* for Sarasvatī, a *caru* for Pūṣan, and a *caru* for Mitra. To the north, [he prepares one] for the chariot-stand (*rathavāhana*). Indeed, he should give this well-yoked chariot as a gift.
They dwell [there].
In the morning he sacrifices with the oblations to the Devikās;
he remains [there], and in the morning he sacrifices with the oblations of the Devasū.
Now he extends this Atirātra sacrifice with all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras;
it has six initiation days, three Upasad days, and the pressing on the tenth day is successfully accomplished through the measuring of the King (Soma).
Having measured out the King (Soma), he divides him into five parts;
therein he explains the Prāṇa-grahas and the eastern spotted ones.
Then, at his midday pressing, having likewise measured out the King, he explains the Apāna-grahas and the northern spotted ones.
The pressing is straightforward;
the cups are drawn in the established manner up to the Āgrayaṇa.
Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws the Atigrāhyas, beginning with the one for Agni with the verse, "O Agni, you purify our lives."
With the verse "Rising up with vigor," which belongs to Indra,
and with the verse "The one who crosses over, visible to all," which belongs to Sūrya—
both are offered as the sacrificial animals for the *atirātra* and the *atigrāhya* cups.
At the Ekādaśinī sacrifice, these animals are to be immolated;

they perform the Rathantara at the Mādhyandina Pavamāna, the Vairāja is the Hotṛ’s Pṛṣṭha-stotra, and during that [stotra], he draws the cup for Mahendra with these two verses: "Great is Indra" and "Thou, O Indra, art great by means of the sacred word."
For he belongs to both: with the two kindling woods and with the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), he introduces the *Māhendra* hymn.
The Udgātṛ rubs that very fire on his chest;
having wrapped it in a cloth and placed a wooden chip between them, once it has been produced, the Udgātṛ utters the *abhihiṅkāra* three times.
He gives it to the *prastotṛ*.
He, having carried it around the north of the *dhiṣṇiya* hearths, hands it to the *adhvaryu* who is seated to the east of the *hotṛ*'s *dhiṣṇiya*.

He, having brought it north of the two *havirdhāna* sheds, south of the *āgnīdhra*, and north of the *āgnīdhrīya* fire, pours it out while saying, "Pouring it out," as follows: "The supporter for the mother, sucking the mother, may he firmly establish for us abundance of wealth, food, and vigor; may the Lord of Prosperity bestow prosperity upon me."
With the words, "May you two be of one mind," he strikes;

with the words, "Fire moves, having entered into fire," he strikes and then offers an oblation; with the words, "Protect me," he worships; and with the words, "Of one mind, of one dwelling—may you two not [be so] today for me."
While they are praising, he attends upon them; having said, "He recites this exclusive *uktha*," he hastens toward the Mahendra cup and offers the *atigrāhya* libations following it.
With the verse addressed to Agni, "O Agni, thou who art resplendent," he offers the oblation with the words, "I offer the resplendent one for the sake of splendor, svāhā!
Then he follows this with the consecratory formula (anumantraṇa), "Thou art the knower of splendor," and [the mantra], "Splendor has indeed come to me."

With the mantra, "O Indra, you who possess vigor," he offers to Indra: "Vigorous, I offer you for the vigor of the kṣatra, svāhā! He follows this with the consecratory formula, "You are the possessor of vigor. [He recites], "May vigor not forsake me; may vigor not be lost.
With the mantra, "O Sūrya, you who possess brilliance," he offers to Sūrya: "Brilliant, I offer you for brilliance, svāhā!"

He consecrates them with the mantra, "Thou art the finder of light"—*śuva-vid asi*. Then, [thinking] "May there be light for thee"—*suvar hāsīt*—he gathers all of these together and, at the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, offers them with the formula, "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!
They then return and consume the portions.
With the verse "May wisdom [be] in me," [he offers] to Agni, [thinking], "May Agni bestow splendor upon me";
with "May wisdom [be] in me," [he offers] to Indra, [thinking], "May Indra bestow power upon me";
and with "May wisdom [be] in me," [he offers] to Sūrya, [thinking], "May he bestow radiance upon me."
The sacrificer himself should consume these;
he introduces the Śākvara chant for the Maitrāvaruṇa with *avakā* plants,
and having crushed them, he mixes the cakes for the third pressing.
Disregarding that, they should lie right here within the limits of the *sadas*. He introduces the *stotra* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin with the *vairūpa* [sāman] using a calf;

he introduces the *stotra* for the Acchāvāka with the *raivata* [sāman] using a cow. They cause the cows and calves to rest together; the cows are on the south side, the calves on the north side. Having brought them together right there between the *sadas* and the *havirdhāna*, they milk them.
They perform the *bṛhat* chant in the place of the *ārbhava-pavamāna*, thinking, "The milk of these [cows] is Agni at the proper time," and he proceeds with the cattle in their proper station.

For these [offerings], there are different *manotās*, different oblations, different touchings, and different deities; however, for all of them, the *vanaspati*, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the *iḍā* for the quarters are entirely common. They lead forward the *ukthas*;
the *ukthas* are successfully accomplished.
He leads forward the *ṣoḍaśin*; the *ṣoḍaśin* is accomplished. He leads forward the night; the night is accomplished.

This Viśvajit sacrifice, characterized by all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras and consisting of an *atirātra*, concludes. There are two barren cows (*vaśā*) dedicated to Viśvakarman and to Sūrya; one of these is to be immolated. There are two *ekakapāla* cakes for Viśvakarman and Sūrya, serving as the animal-offering cakes (*paśupuroḍāśa*). Having performed the ritual with the two omenta (*vapā*), he turns back. Then follows the Vyuṣṭi-dvirātra sacrifice. The first day is an *agniṣṭoma*; he carries forward the oblation of the first day and the second day. Then, one who desires peace should perform the Kṣatrasya Dhṛti sacrifice, an *agniṣṭoma* consisting of four *stomas*. Peace... (text fragmentary).
